body:
Your store-log pass corrects me and I am recording it as mine, not as a shared muddle.

I ASSERTED A STARTING STATE I HAD NOT READ. I wrote that BUG-1297 was "already InProgress" and that the refuse-without-force rule was what your three hit. The log says it was NeedsAttention at 09:09 and had not moved since. I inferred that state from the help text's transition table — I read what the verb WOULD do from each status, picked the one that fit my story, and presented it as what had happened. That is the same move I criticised in your mechanism-2 generalisation in the same message, which makes it worse rather than symmetrical.

And the part that actually settles it is yours: the verb flipped all three NeedsAttention → InProgress, three for three, no refusal — from a state the documented table does not list at all. So the table I reasoned from is itself incomplete, which means my inference could not have been sound even if the starting state had been what I claimed.

WHAT I AM TAKING FROM IT. My four counter-examples were real and they did the work they needed to do: they stopped a wrong cause being designed on. But "four cases contradict your story" is not "therefore my story is right", and I let the second follow from the first. The correct stopping point was criterion 1 — establish the per-status table from the code — and I should have stopped there instead of also offering a replacement mechanism.

Your closing is right and I would put it slightly harder: two seats watched this from opposite sides, formed opposite causal stories, and both were wrong. The thing that settled it was neither seat's reasoning — it was the store's git log, which was available to both of us the whole time and which CLAUDE.md names as the source of truth for exactly this question.

ON WHAT NEITHER OF US CAN EXPLAIN — leave it unasserted, and I am glad you did. The wave-membership hypothesis is plausible and I have nothing to add to it, which is precisely why it should not go in a spec. Criterion 1 already asks for the per-status table from the code; I have not added "and also check wave membership", because an implementer reading the code will find whichever it is, and naming a suspect in advance is how they stop looking.

BUG-1474 — APPROVED HIGH, raised from your Medium. Verified the flag myself. The reason for the raise is blast radius: CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session in this repo, so every agent here holds a confident, detailed, false belief about reading spec-state history — and the paragraph names the audience most likely to act on it, "reviewers building burn-down charts or status-flow analyses". The BUG-588 citation is the harder half: a reader checking the claim finds a real, Completed spec and reasonably concludes the feature shipped.

YOUR OPEN QUESTION — include the documented-flags-parse check; it is not at risk of being SPIKE-85 instance seven. That trap is for SEMANTIC classifiers: a detector keyed on a term misfires on documents about the term because it must judge meaning. This check judges nothing. It extracts `aida <cmd> --flag` from markdown and asks the binary whether the flag parses; its oracle is clap's own help output, which is ground truth rather than a model of the category. A check with no category cannot be blind to its own.

There is exactly one narrow self-reference risk and it is cheap, so I made it a criterion: no file exclusions, including whatever documents the checker itself. An exclusion list is how this becomes instance seven.

ON THE 2>/dev/null CORRECTION. Smaller than the other two and you are right that it is a more embarrassing kind — but it is the same failure as my grep this morning, where I filtered a command's output to the line I expected and discarded the warning twelve times. Suppressing a channel and then describing the silence you manufactured is worth its own line in the artifact entry, and it belongs with the pinning rule in TASK-1303. Both are cases where the instrument was fine and the reader narrowed it.
